entries.requirement: Where a JWT could be confused with another kind of JWT, mitigations against substitution MUST be employed.
entries.notes: Left to the caller: only the application knows which other JWT kinds share its issuer and keys. What the SDK does by default: signature, exp, iss and aud are all checked, and a validator that names no issuer or no audience refuses every token (audit SEC-06; allow_any_issuer / allow_any_audience opt out), so the issuer and audience strategies of 3.12 are on by default once the caller supplies values. Opt-in, NOT default: with_required_typ (typ pin), require_scope, a separate JwtAuthInterceptor and key set per kind of token. With none of the opt-ins, an ID token or any other JWT from the same issuer, with an accepted aud, signed by the same key, is accepted (CONFIRMED: validate() looks at no claim besides exp, nbf, iss, aud, scope, act, sub). See the 3.11 and 3.12 rows. Tests cited assert the default refusal of an unset iss/aud and the typ pin; neither is a cross-JWT-confusion test (no ID-token-as-access-token vector).

entries.requirement: A library MUST let the caller specify the supported algorithm set and MUST NOT use any other algorithm for cryptographic operations.
entries.notes: CONFIRMED trace. validate() (jwt.rs:538) matches header.alg (562-594): only the exact strings HS256, RS256, ES256 reach a crypto operation; every other value (none, None, HS384, PS256, EdDSA, ...) hits `_ => return Err(Rejected)` (593) before any signature is computed. HS256 is checked only against the configured secret (565-571), RS256/ES256 only against key material of that type (verify_asymmetric 1393). The 'MUST NOT use any other algorithm' half holds. The 'MUST enable the caller to specify' half is only implicit: the set is hard-coded, there is no with_algorithms API, and the caller narrows it only through which keys it installs (HS256 iff with_hs256_secret, RS256 iff an RSA key is in the Jwks, ES256 iff an EC P-256 key is); a caller holding an RSA key cannot refuse RS256, nor admit PS256/ES384/EdDSA. Card path (JWS, not JWT): ES256 and EdDSA only, selected the same implicit way through the key handed to verify_agent_card / the JWK Set. Tests: alg_none_is_rejected, none_is_refused_in_every_spelling_and_with_any_signature, algorithm_confusion_rejected, an_hs256_token_signed_with_a_public_key_is_refused, an_hs256_token_with_an_empty_key_is_refused and an_algorithm_name_must_match_exactly assert the 'MUST NOT use any other algorithm' half for none, its spellings, an HS256 MAC keyed with a public key, an empty key, and HS384, HS512, RS384, PS256, ES384, EdDSA and lower-case names; es256/rs256 tests assert the listed algorithms verify. algorithm_confusion_rejected was strengthened on 2026-11-06 (it had never built the confusion token; docs/compliance/control-map.md cites it). The 'caller specifies the set' half has no test because it is not met (the set is hard-coded). Card tests assert RS256 is refused (verify_rejects_unsupported_algorithm, verify_rejects_non_es256_algorithm); no card test presents none, HS256 or ES384.

entries.requirement: The library MUST ensure the alg/enc header names the same algorithm that is actually used for the cryptographic operation.
entries.notes: CONFIRMED trace. validate() reads alg once (jwt.rs:562) and that string selects both the branch and the primitive: HS256 -> ring HMAC-SHA256 (569-571); RS256/ES256 -> verify_asymmetric(alg, key.material, ..) (580-582), whose match pairs (RS256, Rsa) with RSA_PKCS1_2048_8192_SHA256 and (ES256, EcP256) with ECDSA_P256_SHA256_FIXED and returns false for any other pairing (1406-1408). Card path: the key is built for the header alg (VerifyingKey::from_bytes, keys.rs:61), Jwks::candidates_at keeps only keys whose alg equals the header alg (keys.rs:289), and VerifyingKey::verify refuses alg != self.alg() (keys.rs:95). Tests assert correct pairings verify and a wrong key or secret does not. NOT asserted anywhere on the JWT path: a header alg paired with key material of the other type (RS256 header + EC key, ES256 header + RSA key), so the `_ => false` arm of verify_asymmetric is untested. Card path: a_jwks_verifies_by_kid_and_alg refuses an ES256 signature whose kid names an EdDSA key, but two layers (the candidates alg filter and the alg check in VerifyingKey::verify) each cause that refusal alone, so removing the filter leaves it green; the alg check in VerifyingKey::verify is isolated, since 2026-11-06, by a_genuine_signature_is_refused_under_another_algorithms_name (a genuine signature under another algorithm's name; hand mutants: the check disabled, case-insensitive, prefix -> that test fails). a_key_is_never_tried_under_another_algorithm still gives it bogus bytes. Hand mutant to try: make verify_asymmetric's `_ => false` return true and present an RS256 token to an EC-only Jwks.

entries.requirement: Each key MUST be used with exactly one algorithm, and this MUST be checked when the cryptographic operation is performed.
mutant_evidence: VerifyKey::declared_for: the declared algorithm never compared (always true) -> a_key_that_names_an_algorithm_verifies_only_tokens_that_name_it fails; the comparison inverted, made case-insensitive, or the key's alg dropped when the RSA or the EC key is built -> the same test fails
VerifyKey::verifies: the call to declared_for removed -> a_key_that_names_an_algorithm_verifies_only_tokens_that_name_it fails
VerifyKey::declared_for: a key with no alg refused -> a_key_verifies_only_if_use_and_key_ops_allow_it fails

Jwks::from_json: only use:enc skipped (as before 2026-11-06), use compared case-insensitively, key_ops ignored, any non-empty key_ops accepted, key_ops compared case-insensitively or as a prefix, use and key_ops required to both forbid -> a_key_verifies_only_if_use_and_key_ops_allow_it fails
VerifyingKey::verify: the algorithm check disabled, compared case-insensitively or as a prefix -> a_genuine_signature_is_refused_under_another_algorithms_name fails
entries.notes: CONFIRMED and, since 2026-11-06, enforced on both paths. A key's algorithm is fixed by its type (KeyMaterial::Rsa verifies only RS256, KeyMaterial::EcP256 only ES256; verify_asymmetric pairs them) and, new on 2026-11-06, by the JWK's own alg when it names one: Jwks::from_json keeps the member on the key and JwtValidator::validate verifies through VerifyKey::verifies, which asks VerifyKey::declared_for first, so a key that declares RS384, RS512, PS256 or RSA-OAEP (an EC key: anything but ES256) verifies nothing, and the refusal is a rejection, not a key miss (the caller is not told to refetch). Before that date the server read neither alg nor key_ops, skipped only use:enc, and used such a key for RS256 tokens: found by this ledger, fixed with the maintainer's go (decision 2026-11-06, item (a)). from_json also skips a key whose use is present and is not sig, or whose key_ops is present and omits verify (RFC 7517 4.2, 4.3), and refuses a document whose key_ops is not an array of strings. The HS256 secret lives on the validator, is used only in the HS256 branch and never appears in the Jwks, so no key is usable under two algorithms and a public key cannot become an HMAC key. Card path: Jwk::verifying_key refuses use != sig and an alg that contradicts the curve; VerifyingKey::verify refuses alg != self.alg() when the signature is checked, and a_genuine_signature_is_refused_under_another_algorithms_name isolates that check with a genuine signature (the older tests gave it bogus bytes, which fail on their own). NOT done: the card path does not read key_ops (RFC 7517 4.3; the types crate's Jwk has no such member), so a card key set that marks a public key sign-only is still used to verify. That is RFC 7517's SHOULD-level consistency, not this MUST, and it is recorded in docs/handoff.md. The hand mutants behind this row are listed in mutant_evidence; the keys.rs test file builds its controls from the same JWK with the member under test removed, so each refusal is that member's doing.

entries.requirement: A verifier SHOULD treat a JWS as invalid when its algorithm is not acceptable to the application, even if the signature verifies (RFC 7515 5.2).
entries.notes: CONFIRMED. The acceptable set is hard-coded: HS256/RS256/ES256 for tokens (jwt.rs:563-593), ES256/EdDSA for card signatures (VerifyingKey::from_bytes, keys.rs:61-80; Jwks::candidates_at). Anything else is Rejected before a signature is computed, and each listed algorithm additionally needs a key of its type (HS256: a secret set; RS256/ES256: such a key in the set). Tests: alg_none_is_rejected (JWT, lower-case 'none' only); card path verify_rejects_unsupported_algorithm and verify_rejects_non_es256_algorithm (RS256). Not asserted: any other unlisted alg on the JWT path (HS384, RS512, PS256, EdDSA, 'None') and none/HS256/ES384 on the card path.

entries.requirement: Applications MUST only allow cryptographically current algorithms that meet the application's security requirements.
entries.notes: CONFIRMED. Accepted: RS256 through ring's RSA_PKCS1_2048_8192_SHA256 (verified in ring-0.17.14 src/rsa/verification.rs:88-94: moduli under 2048 bits are refused), ES256 on P-256, HS256 with a secret of at least 32 bytes (MIN_HS256_SECRET_LEN, a shorter secret fails closed), and for cards ES256 and Ed25519. No SHA-1, MD5, RS1, HS1, 'none'. The set is not caller-selectable (see the 3.1 row), so the application cannot remove an algorithm it no longer trusts. Tests: the HS256 31/32-byte boundary is asserted (hs256_secret_shorter_than_32_bytes_fails_closed); the valid-token tests show the three algorithms verify. NOT asserted: any RSA key under 2048 bits is refused (no test uses one; changing the ring constant to a 1024-bit variant would pass every test).

entries.requirement: Applications MUST be designed to enable cryptographic agility, so algorithms can change as they weaken.
entries.notes: CONFIRMED. The algorithm set is a constant in the SDK. Within it the application can rotate keys by kid (remote JWKS is refetched on a kid miss, rate limited), mix RS256 and ES256 keys in one JWKS, and swap an HS256 secret. It cannot retire RS256 while keeping an RSA key in the set, nor accept PS256, ES384 or EdDSA tokens (EdDSA exists for agent cards only), without an SDK release. PARTIAL, not APPLICATION, because the SDK narrows what the application can do. The cited test shows key rotation under one algorithm only; nothing exercises changing the algorithm set.

entries.requirement: JWT libraries SHOULD NOT generate JWTs using alg none unless the caller explicitly asks.
entries.notes: The SDK issues no JWTs. The server only verifies; crates/a2a-protocol-client does not mint or parse JWTs (tokens are opaque bearer strings; token_provider/exchange.rs only carries them). The one signer, for agent cards, produces a JWS (not a JWT) whose protected_header (signing.rs:316) is called only with the literals ES256 and EdDSA, so it cannot emit none.

entries.requirement: JWT libraries SHOULD NOT consume JWTs using alg none unless the caller explicitly requests it.
mutant_evidence: JwtValidator::validate: an arm `"none" => true` added to the alg match -> alg_none_is_rejected and none_is_refused_in_every_spelling_and_with_any_signature fail
entries.notes: Stricter than the SHOULD NOT: there is no opt-in, none is always refused. validate() splits on '.', decodes the header, and an alg that is not exactly HS256, RS256 or ES256 falls to `_ => return Err(Rejected)` before the claims are decoded. alg_none_is_rejected builds {alg:none,typ:JWT} with claims that pass every other check and an empty signature; none_is_refused_in_every_spelling_and_with_any_signature adds None, NONE, nOnE, padded and empty spellings, a bogus and a genuine HS256 signature, and three validator configurations (secret and keys, keys only, secret only). Card path: 'none' fails VerifyingKey::from_bytes in verify_agent_card and finds no candidate in verify_agent_card_with_jwks; no card test presents none.

entries.requirement: Applications SHOULD follow the algorithm-specific recommendations: avoid RSA-PKCS1 v1.5 encryption (RFC 8017 7.2), and ECDSA deterministic nonces (next row).
entries.notes: The SDK implements no JWE and no encryption algorithm for tokens: a five-part compact JWE fails the three-part check (jwt.rs:543-546) and a 'key encryption' alg (RSA1_5, RSA-OAEP) is not in the alg match. RS256 is RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, a signature scheme, which this bullet (RFC 8017 7.2 is RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 encryption) does not cover. The ECDSA bullet is the 335 row. No test presents a JWE.

entries.requirement: JWT libraries SHOULD implement ECDSA using the deterministic approach of RFC 6979.
entries.notes: CONFIRMED. The agent-card ES256 signer uses ring's EcdsaKeyPair::sign with a random nonce (ring-0.17.14 src/ec/suite_b/ecdsa/signing.rs:172-192: 'a random nonce generated by rng', hedged by mixing in the digest), not RFC 6979. The test cited asserts the two signatures of one card differ, i.e. it pins the non-determinism; the caching docs recommend Ed25519 or signing once for stable bytes and ETag (audit E-F22), not for nonce quality. This is the card signer, a JWS not a JWT library, and only the signing side: verification is unaffected and the JWT server code signs nothing, so the SHOULD applies by analogy. Mitigations: the nonce comes from the OS CSPRNG via ring::rand::SystemRandom and is hedged; an Ed25519 signer exists. Concrete input: sign_card_es256 twice over one card and key gives two different signatures.

entries.requirement: All cryptographic operations in a JWT MUST be validated, and the whole JWT MUST be rejected if any of them fails.
entries.notes: CONFIRMED trace of the one operation a (non-nested) JWT has: validate() (jwt.rs:538-613) decodes the header, applies the crit and typ refusals, decodes the signature (any base64 failure is Rejected), verifies it (HS256 via ring::hmac::verify, constant time; RS256/ES256 via candidates.iter().any(verify_asymmetric)), and only then decodes the claims (598). Every verification failure returns before claims are read, so no claim of an unverified token is ever used. There is no second operation: JWE and nested JWTs are unsupported (see 346). Card path (a JWS, not a JWT): with keys supplied, ONE valid signature among several suffices (verify_any, signing.rs:700; spec 8.4.3 rotation) and invalid siblings are ignored, a deliberate any-of rule that the JWT compact form, which has one signature, never meets; with NO signature keys configured (the default) nothing is verified at all (discovery.rs:989-991). Tests: HS256 wrong secret, RS256 wrong key, matching-kid bad signature, and a signature computed over a different header (no_kid_bad_signature...) are refused; the fuzz harness unit test forwards_the_token asserts a signature with an extra char and a two-part token are refused. NOT asserted: a bad ES256 signature (es256_valid_and_expired has only a valid and an expired token), a valid signature over a tampered payload on the JWT path, a five-part token, an invalid base64 signature, or that claims are not read before the signature (the order). The fuzz target jwt_token.rs asserts no random input is accepted but runs only under cargo fuzz, not in the test suite.

entries.requirement: For Nested JWTs, both outer and inner operations MUST be validated with the application's keys and algorithms.
entries.notes: Nested JWTs (a JWE wrapping a JWS) are not supported. CONFIRMED refusals: a five-part JWE compact token fails `parts.len() != 3` (jwt.rs:543-546); a JWS whose payload is itself a compact JWT (cty: JWT) has a payload that is not a JSON claims object, so decode_json::<JwtClaims> (598) fails and the token is Rejected, after its outer signature had to verify. The header's cty and zip members are not read (JwtHeader, jwt.rs:710). No test presents a five-part or nested token (grep of the crates' tests for JWE/nested/cty/zip: none); the fuzz unit test forwards_the_token asserts only that the two-part 'a.b' is refused.

entries.requirement: For ECDH-ES with P-256/P-384/P-521, validation of epk inputs MUST follow NIST SP 800-56A r3 5.6.2.3.4.
entries.notes: No JWE and no ECDH-ES anywhere in the SDK (no key agreement code in the auth or signing paths; JwtHeader reads only alg, kid, crit, typ). The nearest analogue is the EC public key used for ES256 verification: the SDK checks only that x and y are 32 bytes each (jwt.rs:225, keys.rs:174-179), and ring validates the point at verification time (ring-0.17.14 src/ec/suite_b/public_key.rs:29-66, on-curve and range checks, called from ecdsa/verification.rs:109), so an off-curve JWK point makes every verification fail. No test presents an off-curve point.

entries.requirement: The key-entropy and random-value advice of RFC 7515 10.1 and the password considerations of RFC 7518 8.8 MUST be followed.
entries.notes: CONFIRMED. What the SDK enforces is the machine-checkable part: an HS256 secret shorter than 32 bytes is never stored (fails closed, every HS256 token is refused; try_with_hs256_secret errors at startup). Entropy cannot be checked and is not: any 32 bytes pass, including [7u8; 32] (used by tests) (the book's samples used the guessable string '0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef' until 2026-11-06; they now show a placeholder for bytes from a secret store, and the validator's rustdoc and the authentication page say a key is random bytes, 'openssl rand -base64 32'). The SDK has no HS256 key generator. Random values: the card signer's ECDSA nonce comes from ring SystemRandom. RFC 7518 8.8 (PBES2 passwords) does not apply: no JWE. Tests assert the 31/32-byte boundary only.

entries.requirement: Human-memorizable passwords MUST NOT be used directly as the key of a keyed-MAC algorithm such as HS256.
mutant_evidence: auth_card::hs256_key returning the text's own bytes, not trimming, reading the URL-safe alphabet, or giving an error that does not name the variable or how to make a key -> the_hs256_variable_is_a_base64_key_used_as_its_bytes or a_typed_passphrase_is_not_a_key fails (5 of 5 hand mutants)
entries.notes: CONFIRMED. with_hs256_secret takes raw bytes and uses them directly as the HMAC key (jwt.rs:569, ring::hmac::Key::new(HMAC_SHA256, secret)): no KDF, no entropy gate, no decoding requirement. The 32-byte floor keeps out short passwords ('hunter2') but a passphrase of 32 or more characters is accepted as the key. The SDK's own example, examples/genai-agent, read A2A_JWT_HS256_SECRET as a string and passed secret.into_bytes() to try_with_hs256_secret, exactly the password-as-key pattern the sentence forbids; since 2026-11-06 it reads the variable as a key in base64 (auth_card::hs256_key, 'openssl rand -base64 32'), so a typed passphrase is refused at startup (not base64) or by the 32-byte floor once decoded, and the book's samples no longer show a guessable string. That fixes the SDK's own use, not the API: with_hs256_secret(b"correct-horse-battery-staple-1234".to_vec()) is still accepted and HS256 tokens under it verify, because the runtime cannot tell a passphrase from a key (the maintainer chose to fix the example and the docs and change no runtime behaviour, 2026-11-06). Tests: the length boundary, and for the example the decoding and the refusal of a typed passphrase and of the old 32-character sample; the wiring in main.rs is covered by a run of the example under probe_auth.py, not by a unit test.

entries.requirement: Compression of data SHOULD NOT be done before encryption.
entries.notes: The SDK encrypts no JWTs and implements no JWE, so there is no compress-then-encrypt path. The JWT/JWS header struct does not read `zip` (JwtHeader, jwt.rs:710-723), so a token claiming compression is never inflated (no decompression-bomb path either). No compression crate sits in the token or card verification path (grep of Cargo.toml: flate2 only as a dev-dependency for the test collector; gzip for OTLP export).

entries.requirement: Implementations MUST use UTF-8 for JSON in headers and claims, and not use or admit other Unicode encodings.
entries.notes: CONFIRMED by reading the code and serde_json 1.0.154 (the locked version): the header and claims are base64url-decoded to bytes and parsed with serde_json::from_slice (jwt.rs:1472-1475), whose SliceRead validates UTF-8 in every string (src/read.rs as_str, 903-913, InvalidUnicodeCodePoint) and does not skip a BOM or UTF-16/32 byte-order or NUL bytes (not JSON whitespace), so such input is a parse error -> Rejected. The card path uses the same call (signing.rs:505, discovery.rs:963-968). A parse error anywhere gives Rejected before any claim is used. NOT tested: no test presents invalid UTF-8, a BOM, or UTF-16/UTF-32 header or claims; signature_header_rejects_malformed_input asserts only an ASCII non-JSON string, bad base64 and a missing alg.

entries.requirement: When a JWT has an iss claim, the application MUST validate that the keys used for its cryptographic operations belong to that issuer.
entries.notes: CONFIRMED. One JwtValidator holds one key source (static Jwks, HS256 secret or one JWKS URL) and a SET of accepted issuers (with_issuer may be called repeatedly; `issuers: HashSet`). The signature is checked against the key source, then iss must be in the set (check_claims_at 657-666): there is no issuer-to-key mapping. Single issuer: the binding holds by construction, and from_oidc_issuer strengthens it (discovery document's issuer must equal the configured one, the validator is bound to it, jwks_uri must be https or loopback). Several issuers (jwt_caller_identity.rs builds exactly that: two issuers, one shared secret) or an HS256 secret next to a JWKS: any holder of any key can mint a token claiming any accepted iss; the with_issuer docs do not say so. For static Jwks and from_jwks_url the application asserts the key/issuer binding by what it installs (app-specific, as the RFC allows). Tests assert the single-issuer binding; none shows that keys are bound per issuer, and one_sub_from_two_issuers_is_two_callers shows the shared-key multi-issuer shape.

entries.requirement: If the keys do not belong to the issuer, the application MUST reject the JWT.
entries.notes: CONFIRMED. Refusals: a signature by a key outside the configured set is Rejected/KeyMiss (validate 575-591); an iss outside the accepted set, or a token with no iss while issuers are configured, is Rejected (check_claims_at 662-665); a validator with no issuer and no allow_any_issuer refuses every token (657-660, SEC-06); from_oidc_issuer binds a validator that names none to the discovered issuer (bind_discovered 1338). Tests: rs256_valid_and_rejections and the HTTP e2e assert RS256_WRONG_KEY (right iss, other key) and RS256_WRONG_ISS (right key, other iss) are refused with the same generic message (I checked the vectors with Python cryptography: RS256_WRONG_ISS and RS256_WRONG_AUD carry valid RS256 signatures under the Jwks key, RS256_WRONG_KEY does not, so each refusal is attributable to the claim or the key alone); unset_audience... asserts an unset issuer refuses a valid HS256 token; the OIDC test asserts a token for another issuer sharing the keys is refused. NOT asserted: a token carrying no iss claim at all against a validator that names an issuer (no vector lacks iss; the `_ => Err(())` arm is untested), iss compared case/trailing-slash-sensitively (exact HashSet match, untested), allow_any_issuer being the only way around.

entries.requirement: When a JWT has a sub claim, the application MUST validate that it is a valid subject or issuer-subject pair at the application.
entries.notes: Left to the caller: JwtValidator has no subject allow-list or hook, and a correctly signed token for an accepted iss and aud authenticates whatever its `sub`. What the SDK does with sub (CONFIRMED, jwt.rs:1060-1065): records the caller identity as jwt:<iss>:<sub>, so one sub from two issuers is two callers and tasks are partitioned per caller; a token with no sub records no identity, which is refused under caller isolation (default) and served only when the application opts into sharing tasks. Deciding whether the subject is valid for the application (account exists, not suspended, issuer-subject pair allowed) is for a custom ServerInterceptor or authorizer reading CallContext::caller_identity. The safe default (isolation) limits what an unknown but validly-signed sub can reach; it does not reject it.

entries.requirement: If the issuer, subject, or issuer-subject pair is invalid, the application MUST reject the JWT.
entries.notes: The issuer half is enforced by the SDK (an unaccepted or missing iss is Rejected, see the 397 row, which carries that status). The subject and the pair are the application's: the SDK has no notion of an invalid subject, so a token whose sub the application does not know is accepted unless a custom interceptor or per-task authorizer refuses it (see the 408 row). The only subject-based refusal the SDK makes is the one under caller isolation for a token with no sub at all.

entries.requirement: If the same issuer issues JWTs for more than one relying party, the JWT MUST contain an aud claim.
entries.notes: This binds the issuer of the JWT, and the SDK issues none (see the 319 row). The verifier side, which is what an SDK server can do, is the 422/424 row: a token with no aud is refused unless allow_any_audience was called (check_claims_at 667-679; `claims.aud.as_ref().is_some_and(..)`).

entries.requirement: The relying party MUST validate the audience, and MUST reject the JWT if aud is absent or not associated with the recipient.
entries.notes: CONFIRMED. aud is read as a string or an array of strings (de_aud 784; any other JSON type fails the claims decode -> Rejected) and must contain, by exact string equality, at least one configured audience (672-678). No aud, an empty array, or no overlap -> Rejected. A validator with no audience refuses every token unless allow_any_audience is called (667-671, SEC-06), and the interceptor logs that at construction (refuses_everything 450). Tests: RS256_WRONG_AUD (valid signature, iss, exp; aud 'other-api'; signature independently confirmed valid under the Jwks key) is refused on the unit and HTTP paths with the generic message, so the refusal is the audience check's; unset_audience... asserts an unset audience refuses a valid token and that allow_any_audience alone does not help while the issuer is unset. NOT asserted: a token with no aud claim (no vector lacks aud; the `is_some_and` None arm is untested), aud as an array containing the accepted value plus others, an empty array, or case sensitivity.

entries.requirement: Applications SHOULD protect against SSRF via jku/x5u headers, e.g. a URL allow-list and no cookies in the key fetch.
mutant_evidence: fetch_jwks: the loop over the card fetch's headers instead of the key fetch's own -> a_key_server_is_never_sent_the_headers_set_for_the_card and a_key_server_is_sent_the_headers_set_for_it fail; sending the card's headers as well as its own -> a_key_server_is_never_sent_the_headers_set_for_the_card fails; sending none -> a_key_server_is_sent_the_headers_set_for_it fails

CardFetchOptions::with_jwks_header writing the card's map, or jwks_headers returning it -> jwks_headers_are_kept_apart_from_the_cards_and_never_printed and a_key_server_is_sent_the_headers_set_for_it fail; Debug printing the values or omitting the names -> jwks_headers_are_kept_apart_from_the_cards_and_never_printed fails
entries.notes: CONFIRMED trace of every header an attacker controls. Server JWT path: JwtHeader (jwt.rs:710-723) deserializes only alg, kid, crit and typ; jku, x5u, jwk and x5c are ignored (serde drops unknown members) and nothing fetches them. kid is only compared by equality with in-memory key ids (Jwks::candidates 254-272), so there is no SQL/LDAP lookup to inject into. The only network fetch a token can cause is a refetch of the CONFIGURED JWKS URL on a kid miss, at most once per 10 s (RemoteJwks::refetch, SEC-04). The URL is fixed at construction or taken from OIDC discovery whose issuer must match and whose jwks_uri must be https or loopback (trustworthy_url, bind_discovered); the JWKS client sends no cookies. Card path: signature_header returns jku as data and nothing in the SDK fetches it (jwks.rs docs say so; fetch_jwks takes the caller's URL, https or literal-loopback http only); x5u and header jwk are never read; header x5c is never read, and a JWK's x5c can only narrow trust (validity and key match, x5c.rs:36), not extend it. Not met as the RFC words it: the caller-chosen JWKS URL is not checked against an allow-list (it is the caller's). The no-cookies half is met: since 2026-11-06 fetch_jwks sends only the headers set for it with CardFetchOptions::with_jwks_header and never the card fetch's with_header values (an Authorization or Cookie set for the card is not sent to the key server; the CLI's card verify sets --header for the key fetch only when it decided the key server is the card's own host or the flag says so); a caller that sets a Cookie with with_jwks_header chose to. A 3xx from a key server is a non-success status and is refused (jwks.rs:113; no redirect code in either HttpsClient). Tests assert the https/loopback rules and the no-refetch-flood; NO test sets jku, x5u, jwk or x5c in a token or card header and asserts that nothing is fetched or trusted, or that a header-embedded jwk is ignored.

entries.requirement: Producers RECOMMENDED to omit the application/ prefix from the typ value (RFC 7515 4.1.9).
entries.notes: Producer-side advice, and the SDK mints no JWTs. Verifier side (CONFIRMED): with_required_typ compares as a media type, ignoring ASCII case and an application/ prefix on either side (normalise_typ 727), as RFC 7515 4.1.9 requires of a recipient; the cited test asserts at+jwt admits AT+JWT, application/at+jwt and Application/AT+JWT and refuses JWT, id+jwt, at+jwt2, xat+jwt, application/jwt and an empty typ.

entries.requirement: The typ value for a Security Event Token SHOULD be secevent+jwt.
entries.notes: The SDK neither issues nor consumes Security Event Tokens (RFC 8417). A caller wanting to validate SETs could use with_required_typ("secevent+jwt"), but nothing in the SDK is SET-specific.

entries.requirement: When explicit typing is used, the media type name RECOMMENDED to have the form application/example+jwt.
entries.notes: Producer-side. The SDK issues no JWT to type. Its docs point callers at at+jwt (RFC 9068) for access tokens (with_required_typ, jwt.rs:398-401); with_required_typ accepts any string. The agent-card signer writes typ JOSE (signing.rs:317, A2A spec 8.4.2): that is a JWS, not a JWT, and the card verifier does not check typ (signature_header ignores it).

entries.requirement: With explicit typing on a Nested JWT, typ MUST be present in the inner JWT.
entries.notes: Nested JWTs are unsupported (see the 346 row): a five-part token fails `parts.len() != 3` and a JWS-in-JWS payload fails the claims decode. With a required typ configured, a token with no typ, or a non-string typ, is refused (typ_accepted 418-429, asserted by a_required_typ_must_match_and_is_otherwise_not_checked).

entries.requirement: Explicit typing is RECOMMENDED for new uses of JWTs.
entries.notes: Left to the caller. The SDK provides the check, with_required_typ("at+jwt") (CONFIRMED: media-type comparison, a missing or non-string typ refused, tested on HS256 tokens; the check runs before the alg dispatch so it is the same for RS256/ES256), but it is NOT the default: without the call typ is not looked at, deliberately, because many issuers sign access tokens with typ JWT or none (doc comment, jwt.rs:405-408). So an ID token with an accepted iss and aud passes by default. The SDK makes no new use of JWTs itself.

entries.requirement: If one issuer can issue several kinds of JWT, their validation rules MUST be mutually exclusive, rejecting JWTs of the wrong kind.
entries.notes: Left to the caller, who knows which kinds exist. Of the RFC's strategies the SDK offers: typ (opt-in), required scope (require_scope), different aud values and different issuers (required, caller-supplied, on by default as a refusal when unset), different keys (one validator and key source per interceptor). It enforces no mutual exclusivity: a default validator accepts any JWT with the right iss, aud and exp signed by the key, whatever its other claims or typ. Note the agent-card JWS shares nothing with this check (alg ES256/EdDSA, payload is the JCS card, typ JOSE not verified), but a key used to sign both cards and JWTs is the application's to avoid (SUSPECTED low: the card verifier ignores typ).

entries.requirement: For new JWT applications, explicit typing is RECOMMENDED.
entries.notes: Same position as the 469 row: with_required_typ exists and works, is opt-in, and the SDK defines no new kind of JWT of its own. See that row for the trace and test.
